conflict_topics: use of shared house fund to buy alcohol
who should reimburse the cost of alcohol
social expectations of guests (Agent B's invited colleagues/boss)
dialogue_quality_notes: Speakers give concrete reasons: D cites discomfort, A cites sunk cost and non-returnable purchase, B cites social expectation (boss), C focuses on fairness of house fund (Turns 6,9,7,10).
Agents articulate trade-offs and possible compromises (Turn 15), keeping discussion substantive rather than evasive.
No role confusion; statements remain consistent with the setting (shared flat, house fund).
evaluation.final_reason: No agreement reached. Agent D consistently objects to alcohol being served in the flat (Turn 6, Turn 11, Turn 13). Other housemates point to sunk costs and guest expectations: Agent A spent ~$150 from the house fund and cannot return the drinks (Turn 9), and Agent B has told colleagues including his boss there would be drinks (Turn 7). Agent C raised that the house fund should not pay for alcohol and suggested A and B cover costs (Turn 10), but no one accepted a concrete settlement. Agent D proposed a compromise (non-alcoholic home party + external drinks) in Turn 15, which Agent A rejected (Turn 16). The incompatible demands (no alcohol at home vs guests expecting/paid-for alcohol) remain unsettled.
position_change_notes: Agent D remained firm in opposing alcohol at the home throughout (Turns 6,11,13).
Agent A initially assumed alcohol was acceptable (bought drinks) and then defended the purchase citing sunk cost and invitations (Turns 1,9,14); A did not accept D's no-alcohol stance by the end.
Agent C shifted focus from asking cost to arguing fairness about the house fund and suggesting A and B should cover costs (Turns 8,10,12), but did not settle the broader norm question.

Agent B raised the practical consequence of guest expectations (Turn 7) and volunteered to help get non-alcoholic drinks earlier (Turn 4), but did not change the central contested positions by the end.

round_scores.evidence: Turn 1 Agent A: 'Oh, I just realised, I didn't get any non-alcoholic drinks... We'll get some juices' and Turn 2 Agent B: 'Yeah, good idea. We'll need some anyway.' — planning only, no disagreement.
Turn 3 Agent A asks for someone to buy non-alcoholic drinks and Turn 4 Agent B volunteers to get them. Cooperative logistics, no conflict introduced.

Turn 5 Agent A asks Agent D preference; Turn 6 Agent D: '...I'm not comfortable with alcohol being at the party here in our home.' This introduces a clear substantive disagreement about whether alcohol should be present in the shared flat.

Turn 7 Agent B: 'Oh. That's a problem. I've invited people from work, including my boss, and I told them there'd be drinks.' and Turn 8 Agent C asks about cost. The disagreement now has practical consequences (guest expectations) and financial stakes, increasing its intensity.

Turn 9 Agent A: '...I used the house fund. It was about $150... shop doesn't take returns.' Turn 10 Agent C: '...the house fund is for things we all share. It's not fair for Agent D's money to pay for alcohol. You and Agent B should cover the cost...' A concrete dispute over who should bear the expense appears alongside D's earlier objection.

Turn 11 Agent D: reiterates discomfort ('it's not about the money. I'm just not comfortable with alcohol being served at the party here'). Turn 12 Agent C: '...we still have to figure out the money.' Two distinct unresolved issues (norms about alcohol at home vs who pays) persist without convergence.

Turn 13 Agent D: '...even if that is sorted, I'm still not comfortable with the alcohol being served here.' Turn 14 Agent A: '...I've already spent about $150... can't return it. And Agent B's told his boss...' Parties are firmly entrenched: D refuses alcohol in the home on principle, others cite sunk cost and social/professional expectations.

Turn 15 Agent D offers a compromise: 'keep the party here non-alcoholic, and maybe you could take your friends for drinks somewhere else after.' Turn 16 Agent A rejects it as inadequate: 'We're still out the money... a bit weird to invite people... especially for Agent B's boss.' The compromise is refused and the core incompatibility persists.

substantive_insights: This is a values vs practicality conflict: Agent D's normative boundary (no alcohol at home) conflicts with others' practical commitments (sunk cost, guests expecting alcohol).
There are two linked but separable disputes: (1) policy about alcohol in the shared home, (2) allocation of sunk cost from the house fund. Both are unresolved.
A proposed accommodation (non-alcoholic home party + external drinks) addresses the normative concern but fails to resolve the sunk-cost/social-expectation problems for others.
